page: Amazon Web Services r6g.2xlarge is an arm64 memory-optimized virtual instance powered by AWS Graviton Neoverse-N1 processors and managed by the Nitro hypervisor. The instance delivers 8 dedicated vCPUs matching 8 physical cores clocked at 2.5 GHz with a single thread per core architecture. It provides 64.0 GB of total RAM, creating an 8.0 GB per core ratio. Hardware accelerators and local disk drives are absent, requiring the use of network-attached Amazon EBS storage alongside a baseline network throughput of 2 Gbps.

Benchmark measurements reflect reliable multi-core throughput and memory bandwidth contrasted against lower single-threaded compute metrics. The instance achieves an uncached read memory bandwidth of 126.06 GB/sec and write bandwidth of 57.75 GB/sec. Application testing demonstrates consistent mid-tier performance with 9.91 million Redis SET operations per second, 5125.24 in PassMark database operations, and 9.9 GB/sec in static web serving. In contrast, workloads dependent on single-threaded execution exhibit weaker results, as seen in a Geekbench single-core score of 961.0, single-threaded gzip compression at 20.31 GB/sec, and reduced LLM token generation rates.

The primary tradeoff of the r6g.2xlarge lies in its emphasis on high memory density and dedicated core isolation rather than high-frequency single-thread compute. The architecture offers efficient resource utilization for memory-heavy operations without hyperthreading contention. Best-fit deployments include in-memory key-value databases such as Redis and Memcached, mid-sized relational database management systems, caching layers, and web application backends requiring substantial memory footprints.
description: Amazon Web Services r6g.2xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual instance built on the 64-bit ARM architecture using AWS Graviton Neoverse-N1 processors on the Nitro hypervisor. The instance provides 8 dedicated physical cores with 8 vCPUs operating at 2.5 GHz, coupled with 64.0 GB of system memory, delivering an 8.0 GB per vCPU allocation. It does not bundle local disk storage or hardware accelerators, utilizing network storage and offering a baseline network speed of 2 Gbps. Benchmark evaluations indicate balanced multi-threaded throughput and steady memory bandwidth, achieving 9.91 million Redis SET operations per second and 126.06 GB/sec in large-block memory reads, offset by lower single-core execution speeds in Geekbench and compression tasks. Without hyperthreading overhead, this hardware configuration provides cost-efficient memory density for caching layers, in-memory databases, and relational data stores.
